en: The Sūtra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Khadiraka, relying upon the site of the Seer Vipaśyin.
At the place where he resided, he was accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
as well as the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa,
with Maitreya at their head. At that time, the Elder Upāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

“World-Honored One, in a previous *Guṇa-sūtra*, you spoke of the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, who is able to eliminate all evil and unwholesome karma, and to cure kings who are outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), even down to śramaṇas who are outcasts, and all those with evil vows (*asaṃvara*). If one wishes to cure such evil conditions, how should one contemplate the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja?”
Even if they were to be seen, how could they dwell together with the Sangha in the performance of the *poṣadha* ceremony?

If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) breaks the five precepts or violates the eightfold fast, or if a renunciant—whether a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, or śikṣamāṇā—violates any of the four grave prohibitions, or if a lay bodhisattva destroys the six fundamental laws, or a renunciant bodhisattva commits one of the eight grave prohibitions: regarding such transgressors, the World-Honored One has previously declared in the Vinaya that they must be definitively expelled, like a great stone shattered to pieces.
Now, in this sutra, it is taught that the Great Compassionate One, Ākāśagarbha, is able to rescue all from suffering, and mantras are taught to eliminate transgressions.
Even if such a person exists, how can one know it?
By what means is this proven?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain it for us.
The Buddha told Upāli:
“You and all those in future ages who properly uphold the Vinaya should instruct these sentient beings who have committed offenses and comfort their minds.”

The World-Honored One’s great compassion and vast vows are immeasurable; never abandoning any being, he has taught in the *Gambhīra-guṇa-sūtra* the method for remedying transgressions, titled the *Vinaya-niścaya*.
There are thirty-five Buddhas, the Great Compassionate Ones who save the world; you should pay them homage.
When you pay homage, you should don the garment of shame and remorse, feeling deep humiliation as if an ulcer had formed in your eye, like a leper following the instructions of a skilled physician.
You should likewise feel shame and remorse.

Once you have felt shame and remorse, for one day up to seven days, prostrate before the Buddhas of the ten directions, recite the names of the thirty-five Buddhas, and specifically recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika Ākāśagarbha.
Having bathed his body and burned various famous incenses, including solid black aloeswood, when the morning star appeared,
he knelt for a long time with palms joined, weeping and shedding tears like rain, and invoking the name of Ākāśagarbha, he said: "O Virtuous One,
O Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva, out of pity for me, please manifest your form before me."
"At that time, one should form this mental image:
upon the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and that wish-fulfilling gem is the color of purple gold."
If one sees the wish-fulfilling jewel, one immediately sees the celestial crown.
Within this celestial crown, thirty-five Buddha images appear; within the wish-fulfilling jewel, the Buddha images of the ten directions appear.
The body of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja is twenty yojanas in height; if he manifests a great body, it is equal to that of Avalokiteśvara.

This bodhisattva sits in the full lotus posture, holding the king of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*) in his hand; from this wish-fulfilling jewel emanate the sounds of all dharmas, which are in accord with the Vinaya.
“If this bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings,

assumes the form of a bhikṣu or any other physical form, and whether in a dream or while practicing dhyāna, seals the arm of that person with a maṇi-jewel seal— whereupon the inscription on the seal reads ‘Removal of Sin’— and having received this inscription, returns to the saṃgha, they shall observe the precepts as before.”
If a lay follower (upāsaka) obtains these words, it shall not hinder his renunciation; even if he does not obtain these words, there shall be a voice in the air proclaiming:
"The offenses are extinguished! The offenses are extinguished!"
If there is no voice from the void to inform one of the *vinaya*, one shall see the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha in a dream, who will say:
“*Vinaye vinaye*, [the offense of] such-and-such a bhikṣu and such-and-such an upāsaka must be further repented.”
"If you prostrate before the thirty-five Buddhas for one day up to seven weeks, by the power of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, your offenses will be lightened.
O Knower of the Dharma!"
He further instructed him to plaster and repair the latrines for eight hundred days.
Day after day he said to him:
"You have committed an impure act; now, with single-minded focus, plaster all the latrines so that no one knows of it."
Having anointed yourself and bathed, prostrate before the thirty-five Buddhas and invoke the name of Ākāśagarbha.
Facing the twelve divisions of the sūtras, cast your body flat on the ground and confess your transgressions and evils.
Having performed repentance in this manner for another three weeks, the wise person should then assemble close friends and relatives before an image of the Buddha.

They should recite the names of the thirty-five Buddhas, invoke Mañjuśrī, and invoke the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa to serve as witnesses. Then, they should perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) once more, according to the method for receiving the precepts as previously described.
"By the power of this person's ascetic practices, their karmic offenses will be forever eliminated, and they shall not be hindered from the three types of bodhi-karma.
The Buddha told Upāli:

"You should uphold this Dharma of Contemplating the Space Treasury and explain it in detail for the sake of sentient beings in future ages who lack shame and remorse and frequently commit evil deeds."
When these words were spoken, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha sat cross-legged, emitting golden light; having seen the thirty-five Buddhas within a wish-fulfilling jewel, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This wish-fulfilling jewel of mine emerges from the Śūraṃgama; therefore, any sentient being who beholds this jewel shall obtain the sovereign mastery of their wishes.
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded Upāli:
"You must uphold this sutra, but you must not preach it extensively to a large multitude."

"However, for the sake of a single person who upholds the Vinaya, and so that he may serve as eyes for the sentient beings of future ages who are without eyes, you must be careful not to forget or lose it.
When Upāli heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Appendix to the Right: Regarding the *Guan xukongzang pusa jing* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha), according to the *Kaiyuan lu*, this is a single-translation text consisting of only two sheets.

Following the sūtra, there were originally eight additional pages of scriptural text; however, based on the collation notes by Master Zhutang regarding the Tripitaka, these appear to be later compilations of the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* dhāraṇīs, as well as the names of Buddhas and dhāraṇīs from various other sūtras, intended as methods for exhorting the world toward practice. Consequently, they should not be appended to the end of the *Guan xukongzang jing*. Neither the lower-Zhu edition nor the Fu edition contains them.
Furthermore, according to this sutra, the World-Honored One previously expounded the method for remedying transgressions in the *Gambhīra-guṇa-sūtra*, titled the *Niyata-vinaya*.

As for the thirty-five Buddhas, they appear in the ninth volume of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, in the "Upāli-parivarta," which shares the same textual basis as the *Niyata-vinaya-sūtra*; all other passages follow this same pattern.

However, upon carefully examining the principles set forth in the critique, they can also be understood through intuitive insight; since they merely appear plausible, I have provisionally deleted them.

Various diseases afflict their bodies, their minds become distracted, they are deaf, blind, mute, or lack various sense faculties; their limbs and joints are deformed, and at times they exhibit signs of death—such things as these.

Constantly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha for the sake of eliminating all illnesses and desiring freedom from disease; burn aloeswood, black hard aloeswood, or tagara incense, and pay homage to the Great Good Man Ākāśagarbha.

This virtuous man, appearing in the form of a brahmin within the patient's dream at night, will manifest before them as the image of Śakra, the image of Puṇyavatī, or the image of Mañjughoṣa; or he may appear in the form of a rākṣasa, a high minister, a military official, a medicinal herb, or their own parents. Appearing thus before the sick person in the dream at night, he will explain various decoctions and medicines appropriate to the illness exactly as they are; upon taking a single dose, the ailment will be completely cured without remainder.

Furthermore, there are those who engage in such pursuits as seeking worldly affairs, desiring to inquire extensively about the meaning of the Dharma, or desiring to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a secluded place; desiring wisdom; desiring fame; desiring skillfulness; desiring sovereignty; desiring a beautiful appearance; desiring land grants; desiring power; desiring wealth and capability; desiring a melodious voice; desiring offspring; desiring a retinue; desiring merit; or desiring to attain the virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.
Desiring meaningful speech, desiring to be honored by others, and desiring to be liberated from all evils and calamities, one should abide in giving, up to and including abiding in wisdom.
Desiring long life and desiring various necessary requisites so that they may be obtained and utilized, one should practice these virtues.

If this person pays homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha—whether in a forest hermitage, within a grove, or on a path—and burns aloeswood, black hard aloeswood, or tagara incense; with a sincere heart, joining their palms and prostrating themselves fully upon the ground, they should pay homage throughout the ten directions and recite the dharani phrases. Thus, they shall immediately obtain their aspirations.

Those who hear the names of these fifty-three Buddhas shall not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Furthermore, if there are those who can recite the names of these fifty-three Buddhas, they will always encounter the Buddhas of the ten directions in every place where they are born.

If there are those who can, with a sincere heart, pay respectful homage to the names of these fifty-three Buddhas, they shall eliminate the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the slandering of the Vaipulya sutras, such that all are completely purified.

Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, Śākyamuni Buddha; to the east, Ratnaprabhācandramaṇḍala-svararāja Buddha; to the south, Vṛkṣamūlapuṣparāja Buddha; to the west, Nirmāṇarāja-ṛddhyarcispuṣpa Buddha; to the north, Candramaṇḍalaviśuddha Buddha; below, Suśānticandrarutārāja Buddha; above, Anantavīryapraṇidhānaśirṣa Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnajāla: "If there are good sons or good daughters..."
He erected a lecture hall as vast as a trichiliocosm.
Within this hall, he constructed billions of viharas, all fashioned from red sandalwood.

Having made offerings to all Buddhas with every kind of requisite for happiness throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, and after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, he further erects stūpas and temples, adorned with banners, streamers, flower canopies, precious vases, incense burners, musical instruments, songs, and praises.
"What do you think?
Is the merit of this person not indeed great?
Jewel Net replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“It would not equal the merit of someone who recites, remembers, and pays reverent homage to the names of these Buddhas of the six directions.”
In every lifetime, such a person will always be born into the family of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), endowed with handsome features and majestic virtue;
when their life is about to end, ten billion Buddhas will extend their hands to receive them, ensuring they do not fall into the three evil realms.

Should one have committed the five grave offenses of immediate retribution (ānantarya) that would otherwise lead to rebirth in hell, these shall be made to be experienced lightly in the present life; by suffering a headache instead, they shall be expiated, and one shall not enter the three evil realms to undergo such retribution.
"Therefore, with a sincere heart, pay homage with reverence. Thus he extensively expounded the *Ratnajālaputra Sūtra*.

If a bodhisattva violates the first precept, they should perform a solemn repentance with a straightforward mind before ten members of the assembly;
if they violate a precept with their own hands, they should perform a solemn repentance with a straightforward mind before five members of the assembly;
if they take hold of a woman with an evil mind upon seeing her, they should perform a solemn repentance with a straightforward mind before one or two persons.

If there is a bodhisattva who commits the five ānantarya offenses, or violates a woman, or violates a man, or commits a manual offense, or offends against a stūpa, or offends against the Saṃgha, or other such transgressions.
A bodhisattva should, in the presence of the thirty-five Buddhas, repent with a sincere mind while dwelling alone day and night for the grave offenses they have committed.
As for the method of repentance: take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha.

These fourteen bodhisattvas— Ghoṣadatta from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, those who wish to come and behold [the Buddha],
and those who would gain worldly blessings by recollecting and paying homage to him—
namely, Citracaryā Bodhisattva, Apramāṇacaryā Bodhisattva, Viśuddhacaryā Bodhisattva, and Pratisthitacaryā Bodhisattva.
Those who recite the names of these four bodhisattvas and pay them homage with mindfulness shall not pass through the three evil realms at the end of their lives.

They are: the Bodhisattva Emptiness-Non-existence in the East, the Bodhisattva Skillful Contemplation in the South, the Bodhisattva Joyful Faith-Purity in the West, and the Bodhisattva Flower of Supernatural Powers in the North.
By recollecting and paying homage to these four bodhisattvas, one attains the merit of the three periods of time and proceeds toward the path of Buddhahood:
Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Ratnākara, Bodhisattva Guhagupta, Bodhisattva Naradatta, Bodhisattva Susīma, Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva Indradatta, and Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva.
These eight bodhisattvas emerged from the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*. These eight individuals have sought the Way for incalculable kalpas, yet they have not yet attained Buddhahood.
I make this vow:
"May all the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions attain the path of Buddhahood.
Should anyone suffer from urgent illness, if they call upon the names of us eight persons, they shall immediately obtain liberation."
"At the time when my life comes to an end, these eight persons shall fly forth to welcome and receive me.
By reciting and paying homage to these eight bodhisattvas, one obtains blessings in the present life;
at the end of life, these eight will come to welcome one, leading one to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to be born by transformation within a lotus flower as an unborn bodhisattva.
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Subhūti—
those who recollect and pay homage to these four śrāvakas shall cause others to obtain blessings in the present life.
"Pūrṇa, Ānanda, and Rāhula, you śrāvaka disciples!
These three provisional śrāvakas—those who recollect and pay homage to them—will cause people to attain the merit of the Mahāyāna."

Among these eight stūpas on earth, reciting their names and paying homage likewise enables people to obtain blessings in the present life.

*Sarvasara-samanvabaddha-paṭipaṭi-mahā-anāśāya svāhā.* At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, when I was still an ordinary person, my name was Cāṭadhara. I lived in the kingdom of Kālūṇa, where I made my living as a merchant engaged in trade."
Deceptive and devoid of reality, he committed innumerable evil deeds;
his licentiousness and lack of principle cannot be fully described.
At that time, out of folly, he harmed his father and loved his mother; after several years had passed, all the people throughout the land knew of it.
They cried out in unison:
"This is Cāṇūra, who murdered his father and violated his mother; it has been several years now.
At that time, I thought to myself: "He is no different from the six domestic animals; he possesses no human qualities whatsoever."
At that time, in the kingdom of Kāruṇya, he leaped over the city walls and fled toward a deep forest.
Then the king of this land, named Viśākha, issued a proclamation to the people of the realm:
"This Cāṭadatta is licentious, depraved, and devoid of the Way; it is because of him that this matter has come to pass."
"Whoever is able to capture this man shall be granted a generous reward of precious goods.
At that time, the people of this country each accepted the recruitment, desiring to seize my person.
At that time, struck with terror, he immediately left his country to become a śramaṇa.
In another land, he practiced the ten wholesome paths, sat in meditation to study the Way, and wept day and night.
After thirty-seven years, because of the karmic obstructions of the five heinous crimes, his mind was not at peace and he could not endure his grief and sorrow.
During those thirty-seven years, while staying in a mountain cave, he constantly wept aloud, crying:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! With what mind shall I depart from this suffering?
Having lamented thus, he descended into the cave to beg for food.
At that time, on the road, he found a large alms bowl containing a single casket of scriptures. There were no other scriptures;

there was only the *Dhāraṇī of the Accumulation of Dharma-Joy for the Abandonment of Suffering*, which describes how, when past Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges entered parinirvāṇa, they always remained in the kingdom of Vaidiśa and preached this dhāraṇī, entrusting it to the great bodhisattvas.
If there are those who later hear this dhāraṇī, it is because in their past lives they practiced the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, whereby they have now been enabled to hear it.
If there are those who hear this yet do not take it to heart or cultivate it through practice, they are said to be without the necessary conditions.
This dhāraṇī can eliminate the great sins of the five heinous acts and the cycle of birth and death for ten billion kalpas.
If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, they shall never fall into the three miserable realms—hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Why is this? Because when the Buddhas of the past were about to enter *nirvāṇa*, they invariably spoke of it.
They shall revere, praise, and look up to him, extolling his meritorious virtues beyond measure.
Entrusting this to the Bodhisattvas, any sentient beings hereafter who hear this dhāraṇī and cultivate it with a devoted mind will find their karmic rewards difficult to calculate.
It is like the jewel-sea of Mount Sumeru, which ordinary people cannot fathom.

If there is someone who has committed various evil deeds, yet hears the name of this dhāraṇī in secret— even if they do not practice it but merely keep it once in their heart— and should fall into hell, then within all the hells,
the suffering shall not be inflicted upon them by virtue of this person's merit.

If there are those capable of practicing it, who attain it through diligent cultivation in their present bodies, they shall behold hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-fields and obtain immeasurable merit that cannot be fully described.
Only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to exhaustively master it; those of the two vehicles, the Śrāvakas, cannot know it.
Why is this? This dhāraṇī was not spoken by one Buddha or two Buddhas, but was spoken by as many Buddhas of the past as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
"At that time, having obtained this sutra, I immediately ceased begging for alms and joyfully proceeded toward my cave.
Upon reaching the cave, I burned incense and prostrated, praising and looking up to it with tears of sorrow."
While practicing recitation within the cave, it was only after one year that I finally attained it;
yet, due to the obstructions of my karmic offenses, I could not cause it to enter my heart.
At that time, during an autumn night, I bathed and practiced for seven days, like a child first learning—there was no small amount of confusion and difficulty.
He practiced for another seven days, yet it remained as chaotic and no different from before.
Distressed in his heart and not knowing what to do, he focused his thoughts upon the syllables of this dhāraṇī; after reciting them several times, his mind suddenly became settled.
At that time, I was filled with joy, like a person who finds a hundred thousand catties of gold in the earth while no one else knows of it;
my inner delight did not cease, and I was just the same.
After practicing for several years, I attained unimpeded power of flight.
Behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Hereafter, any practitioner who acts in accordance with the Dharma shall do so.

The Dhāraṇī Mantra of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva: *Namo buddhānāṃ* *Mahāmoggallāna svāhā* *Tadyathā: kili kili mili cili sarvagākili mili sarvagāmili svāhā.* Regarding this dhāraṇī: on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, when the morning star appears, one should recite it eight hundred times while burning fine aloeswood incense, ensuring the smoke does not cease. One must also use eight hundred yellow flowers. This will cause people to obtain blessings.
If it be a good man!
His present body shall be at peace and secure; whatever he seeks in his heart, there shall be nothing he does not obtain.
If it be a woman!
They shall be transformed into men.

If one can, with a sincere heart, practice the Way for one day and one night across six periods, reciting and upholding [this], the sins of one or two kalpas will never again cause entry into the evil realms.
One should practice during the cool seasons of spring and autumn: specifically in the third, fourth, eighth, and ninth months.
See the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
